title: Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
summary: A complete working grammar for SSC: parts of speech, tenses, subject-verb agreement, articles, prepositions, conjunctions, modals, conditionals, comparison, question tags, non-finites and inversion. It is rarely asked by name, but it decides roughly 7 Tier 1 questions (error spotting, sentence improvement, fill in the blanks, voice and narration) and about 10 in Tier 2.

subtopics.title: Parts of speech: nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs
subtopics.concept:
Every error-spotting question is really asking **which word is doing the wrong job**. Start by knowing the eight jobs.

| Part of speech | Job in the sentence | Example (word in bold) |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | names a person, place, thing, idea | **Honesty** pays. |
| Pronoun | replaces a noun | **She** called **us**. |
| Adjective | describes a noun/pronoun | a **brave** soldier |
| Verb | action or state | He **writes**; she **is** tired. |
| Adverb | modifies verb/adjective/adverb | runs **fast**, **very** tall |
| Preposition | links noun to rest of sentence (place, time, relation) | sat **on** the wall |
| Conjunction | joins words/clauses | tea **or** coffee; **although** it rained |
| Interjection | sudden feeling | **Alas!** he is gone. |

### Nouns that SSC loves
| Group | Words | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Uncountable (no plural, no a/an) | information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, scenery, poetry, stationery, jewellery, evidence, knowledge, mischief, traffic, bread | singular verb; use *a piece of / an item of* to count: *two pieces of advice* |
| Always plural | scissors, trousers, spectacles, tongs, pliers, thanks, alms, premises, riches, outskirts, surroundings, belongings, proceeds | plural verb; *a pair of scissors* takes a singular verb |
| Singular form, plural meaning | cattle, police, people, poultry, clergy, gentry, vermin, peasantry | plural verb: *The police **are** investigating.* |
| Plural form, singular meaning | news, mathematics, physics, economics (subject), civics, measles, mumps, billiards | singular verb: *The news **is** good.* |
| Same singular and plural | sheep, deer, swine, series, species, aircraft | number shown by determiner/verb: *a series is*, *two series are* |
| Number words after a definite number | dozen, hundred, thousand, million, score, lakh, crore, pair | no -s: *three dozen eggs, five hundred rupees*; but *dozens of*, *hundreds of* |
| Number + noun used as adjective | a five-year plan, a ten-rupee note, a two-hour delay | hyphenated, noun stays singular |

**Collective nouns** (team, committee, jury, family, audience, crowd, army): singular verb when the group acts **as one unit** (*The committee **has** approved the plan*), plural when members act **individually** or disagree (*The jury **were** divided in their opinions*).

**Possessive case**
- Living things take *'s*: *the minister's car*. Non-living things take *of*: *the leg of the table* (not *the table's leg*).
- Exceptions (time, distance, weight, personified things): *a day's leave, a stone's throw, a kilo's weight, the nation's pride*.
- Joint ownership: *Ram and Shyam's shop* (one shop). Separate ownership: *Ram's and Shyam's shops*.

### Pronouns
| Situation | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| After a preposition (between, for, with, to, like) | object form: me, him, her, us, them, whom | *between you and **me***, *for him and **me*** |
| After *than / as* | the form the hidden verb needs | *He is taller than **I** (am)*; *I like you more than **him*** (than I like him) |
| After *let* | object form | *Let **him and me** try.* |
| Complement of *be* (formal) | subject form | *It is **I**.* |
| Order of persons (normal) | 2nd, 3rd, 1st (**231**) | ***You, he and I** will go.* |
| Order when admitting fault | 1st, 2nd, 3rd (**123**) | ***I, you and he** are to blame.* |
| Subject *one* | one's / oneself | *One must keep **one's** promises.* |
| Reflexive after *avail, absent, pride, enjoy (oneself), apply (effort)* | needs -self | *He **availed himself of** the offer.* |

- **-self pronouns are never subjects**: *My friend and myself went* ✗ → *My friend and **I** went*.
- **Who / whom / whose / which / that**: *who* = subject (people), *whom* = object (people), *whose* = possession, *which* = things. Use **that** after superlatives, *all, only, same, none, nothing, everything*: *the best book **that** I have read*.
- **Either / neither** refer to two; **any / none** to more than two. SSC keys follow the traditional rule *each other* (two) and *one another* (more than two).
- A pronoun must have **one clear antecedent** and agree with it in number: *Each of the girls brought **her** bag.*

### Adjectives
| Pair | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| few / a few / the few | *few* = hardly any (negative), *a few* = some, *the few* = all of the small number | *The few books he had were old.* |
| little / a little / the little | same idea for uncountables | *There is **little** hope* (almost none). |
| many / much | countable / uncountable | *many chairs, much furniture* |
| fewer / less | countable / uncountable | ***fewer** people, **less** sugar* |
| elder, eldest / older, oldest | *elder* only for family, before a noun, never with *than* | *my **elder** sister*; *she is **older than** me* |
| later, latest / latter, last | time / order | *the **latest** news; the **latter** half* |
| farther / further | distance / additional | *two km **farther**; **further** details* |

- **Order of adjectives (OSASCOMP)**: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose: *a **beautiful small old round brown Indian wooden** dining table*.
- **Absolute adjectives** are not compared: unique, perfect, ideal, complete, entire, round, square, supreme, universal. *more unique* ✗.

### Adverbs
- **too** = more than needed (negative result): *too weak **to** walk*. **very** = high degree: *very weak*.
- **enough** comes after the adjective/adverb: *old **enough***, *fast **enough***.
- **hardly, scarcely, barely, seldom, rarely** are already negative: *I can **hardly** hear* ✓, *I can't hardly hear* ✗.
- Look-alike pairs: *hard* (with effort) / *hardly* (almost not); *late* / *lately* (recently); *near* / *nearly* (almost); *high* / *highly* (very much).
- Linking verbs (look, seem, feel, smell, taste, sound, appear, become, grow) take an **adjective**, not an adverb: *The soup tastes **good*** (not *well*); *She looks **sad***.
- **very** with positive degree and *-ing* adjectives; **much** with comparatives and many past participles: *very tall, very interesting; **much** taller, **much** obliged*.
- Frequency adverbs go **before the main verb** but **after *be***: *He **always** comes late*; *He is **always** late*.

tricks.title: Pronoun case test: cover the other name
tricks.body: When a pronoun is paired with a noun (*Ravi and I / Ravi and me*), cover the noun and read the sentence with the pronoun alone. *The teacher praised ~~Ravi and~~ me* ✓ because *praised me* sounds right; *praised I* does not.

example.q: The award was shared by Meena and ___ . (I / me)
example.solution: Cover *Meena and*: *shared by me*. After the preposition *by* we need the object form **me**.

tricks.title: Noun trap scan
tricks.body: In any error-spotting sentence, circle every noun and ask two questions: *Is it countable?* and *Is it one of the special groups (uncountable / always plural / cattle-type)?* About one in five SSC noun errors is *informations, furnitures, advices, sceneries, luggages*.

example.q: Spot the error: He gave me / some useful advices / before the interview.
example.solution: *advice* is uncountable, so **some useful advice**. If a count is needed: *two pieces of advice*.

tricks.title: Few vs a few: the half-glass rule
tricks.body: *few / little* = the glass is **empty** (negative feeling); *a few / a little* = there is **something** (positive feeling). If the sentence continues with a negative idea (*so he could not...*), pick *few/little*; if positive (*so he managed...*), pick *a few/a little*.

example.q: He had ___ friends in the new city, so he felt lonely. (few / a few)
example.solution: Loneliness is the negative result, so **few** (hardly any).

mistakes: Pluralising uncountable nouns: *furnitures, informations, luggages, sceneries, equipments*.
Using *myself* as a subject: *Ravi and myself will attend* ✗.
Writing *elder than*; the comparative with *than* is always *older than*.
Using *less* with countable nouns: *less mistakes* ✗ → *fewer mistakes*.
Adding a second negative to *hardly/scarcely*: *I could not hardly breathe* ✗.
Adding *-s* to *dozen/hundred/lakh* after a number: *five hundreds rupees* ✗.
subtopics.notes:
### Why parts of speech decide marks
Every error-spotting item is really asking *which word is doing the wrong job*. A noun sits where a verb should be, or an adjective where an adverb is needed. If you know the job each slot needs, the error announces itself.

### Uncountable nouns: the biggest trap family
These nouns have **no plural** and take **singular** verbs, and *much / little / a little* go with them:
information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, news, machinery, equipment, scenery, poetry, jewellery, hair, work, bread, money, traffic, progress.
- *She gave me many advices* → **some advice**.
- *The furnitures are new* → **the furniture is new**.
- *The news were shocking* → **the news was shocking**.
*Many* goes with countable plurals (many friends); *much* with uncountables (much time).

### Word-form families
Exams love slots that need one particular form of a family. Check what the slot **needs**:
| Needed | Signal in the sentence | Example |
|---|---|---|
| noun | after *the / his / of / key to* | hard work leads to **success** |
| adjective | before a noun, after *the / very* | his **courteous** behaviour |
| adverb | after an action verb, or modifying an adjective | spoke **harshly**; highly **successful** |
| verb | after the subject or a modal | he will **succeed** |

Common families: succeed–success–successful–successfully; courage–encourage–courageous; strength–strengthen–strong; beauty–beautify–beautiful; anger–angry–angrily.

### Adjective or adverb?
- After an **action verb**, use an adverb: *She sings beautifully.*
- After a **linking verb** (be, seem, look, feel, smell, taste, sound, appear), use an adjective: *The soup tastes good*, not *goodly*.
- Careful: *look* can do both — *He looked sad* (seemed) vs *He looked sadly at the dog* (gazed).

### Pronoun jobs
- **Subject** pronouns act: I, we, he, she, they. **Object** pronouns receive: me, us, him, her, them.
  *Between you and **me*** (after a preposition); *Rahul and **I** went* (as subject).
- **Possessive adjective** before a noun: its employees. **Its** never takes an apostrophe; *it's* = it is.
- *One... one's*; *each other* for two, *one another* for more than two (the classic exam pair).

### Quick revision
- Uncountables never take -s: information, advice, furniture, news, luggage, machinery.
- much + uncountable; many + countable plural.
- Slot decides the form: of/to/for + noun; before noun + adjective; action verb + adverb.
- Linking verbs take adjectives: tastes good, feels bad.
- Between you and me; its without apostrophe; each other (two), one another (many).

patterns.name: Uncountable noun trap
patterns.howToSpot: A pluralised uncountable (advices, furnitures, informations) or a much/many mismatch.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask: can I count this noun in units?
2. Uncountable → no plural -s, singular verb, much/little.
3. Rewrite the part and match the option that carries the uncountable form.

*Why it works:* the exam reuses the same small list of uncountables every year.

example.q: *Parts: She gave me / many useful advices / before the interview. / No error*
example.solution: **many useful advices** is the error — advice is uncountable → *some useful advice*.

patterns.name: Word-form family choice
patterns.howToSpot: A blank sits before a noun, after a preposition, or after an action verb; the four options are the four forms of one family.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide what the slot needs: noun, adjective, adverb or verb.
2. Find the signal (the/his/of → noun; before a noun → adjective; after an action verb → adverb).
3. Pick the option with that form.

*Why it works:* only one family member fits the slot's job.

example.q: *Hard work is the key to ___.* (succeed/success/successful/successfully)
example.solution: 'to' after key works as a preposition → noun → **success**.

patterns.name: Linking verb + adjective
patterns.howToSpot: The verb is be, seem, look, feel, smell, taste or sound, and one option is an -ly adverb.
patterns.logic:
1. Test the verb: can it be replaced by 'is/ seems'? Then it is a linking verb.
2. Linking verb + adjective (describes the subject).
3. Reject the adverb option.

*Why it works:* the adjective describes the subject's state, not the manner of the verb.

example.q: *The flowers smell ___.* (sweet/sweetly)
example.solution: Smell here = 'are when smelled' → adjective → **sweet**.

patterns.name: Pronoun case and agreement
patterns.howToSpot: A pronoun follows a preposition (between you and ___), acts as subject, or must agree with its owner (the company and ___ decision).
patterns.logic:
1. Find the pronoun's job: subject, object or owner.
2. Object job or after a preposition → me/him/them; subject job → I/he/they.
3. Owner job → its/his/their + noun, never it's.

*Why it works:* case is fixed by the job, not by the sound.

example.q: *Between you and ___, the plan is weak.* (me/I)
example.solution: After the preposition 'between' → object form → **me**.

subtopics.title: Tenses and sequence of tenses
subtopics.concept:
### The 12 tenses at a glance
| Tense | Form | Main use | Signal words | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Simple present | V1 / V1+s | habits, facts, timetables | always, usually, every day | The sun **rises** in the east. |
| Present continuous | is/am/are + V-ing | action now; fixed near-future plan | now, at present, look! | She **is writing** a report. |
| Present perfect | has/have + V3 | past action with present result; unspecified time | just, already, yet, ever, never, so far, recently | I **have finished** my work. |
| Present perfect continuous | has/have been + V-ing | action started in past and still continuing (with duration) | since, for, how long | He **has been waiting** for two hours. |
| Simple past | V2 | finished action at a stated past time | yesterday, ago, last year, in 2010 | We **met** him last week. |
| Past continuous | was/were + V-ing | action in progress at a past moment | when, while, at 8 pm yesterday | I **was reading** when you called. |
| Past perfect | had + V3 | earlier of two past actions | before, after, already (past) | The train **had left** before we reached. |
| Past perfect continuous | had been + V-ing | past action continuing up to another past point | for, since (in past) | She **had been working** there for ten years when she resigned. |
| Simple future | will/shall + V1 | future fact, decision, prediction | tomorrow, next week, soon | I **will call** you tomorrow. |
| Future continuous | will be + V-ing | action in progress at a future moment | at this time tomorrow | We **will be travelling** at noon tomorrow. |
| Future perfect | will have + V3 | action completed before a future point | by, by the time, by then | By March, they **will have completed** the bridge. |
| Future perfect continuous | will have been + V-ing | duration up to a future point | for ... by | By June, he **will have been teaching** for 20 years. |

### Ten tense rules behind most SSC errors
1. **since + point of time, for + period of time**, and both normally need a **perfect** tense: *I **have lived** here **since** 2019 / **for** six years* (not *I live here since 2019*).
2. **Future time clauses take the simple present**: after *when, if, unless, until, till, before, after, as soon as, once, in case*, do not use *will*: *I will call you when he **arrives*** (not *will arrive*).
3. **Definite past time words forbid the present perfect**: *I **saw** him yesterday* ✓; *I have seen him yesterday* ✗.
4. **Earlier of two past actions → past perfect**: *The patient **had died** before the doctor came.*
5. **Sequence of tenses**: a past reporting/main verb pushes the subordinate clause into the past: *He said that he **was** busy.* Exception: universal truths and habitual facts stay present: *The teacher said that water **boils** at 100 °C.*
6. **Stative verbs are not used in continuous tenses**: know, believe, understand, like, love, hate, want, prefer, own, possess, belong, contain, consist, seem, mean, see, hear, smell (involuntary). *I **know** him* ✓; *I am knowing him* ✗.
7. ***It is time / It is high time / It is about time* + subject + past form**: *It is high time we **left**.*
8. **Two linked past events with hardly / scarcely / no sooner** use past perfect in the first clause and simple past in the second: *No sooner **had** I **reached** the station **than** the train **left**.*
9. ***By the time* + present → future perfect**; ***by the time* + past → past perfect**: *By the time you **arrive**, I **will have left***; *By the time we **arrived**, the show **had begun***.
10. ***It is / has been* two years since** + simple past: *It is two years since he **left** the job.*

### Tense consistency
Keep one time frame inside a sentence unless the meaning changes: *She **opened** the door and **sees** a stranger* ✗ → *saw*.

tricks.title: Signal-word scan
tricks.body: Before reading options, underline the time signal: *since/for* → perfect; *yesterday/ago/last/in 2019* → simple past; *by + future time* → future perfect; *when/if/as soon as + future meaning* → simple present; *before/after* joining two past events → past perfect for the earlier one.

example.q: She ___ (work) in this bank for eight years now.
example.solution: *for eight years now* = started in past, still continuing → **has been working** (present perfect continuous).

tricks.title: The 'no will after when/if' reflex
tricks.body: If a clause begins with *when, if, unless, until, as soon as, before, after, once* and talks about the future, strike out *will/shall* in that clause. The *will* belongs only to the main clause.

example.q: Spot the error: Unless you will apologise, / she will not / speak to you again.
example.solution: Clause after *unless* refers to the future → simple present: **Unless you apologise**.

mistakes: Using present perfect with a past time marker: *has gone yesterday*.
Using *will* in *if/when/unless* clauses about the future.
Writing *since two years*; *since* needs a point of time, *for* needs a duration.
Using stative verbs in -ing form: *I am understanding the problem* ✗.
Changing a universal truth to past in reported speech: *said that the earth moved round the sun* ✗.
Using simple past for the earlier of two past actions when *before/after* is not present to show order clearly.
subtopics.notes:
### The four zones
English tenses divide time into four zones — simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous — across past, present and future. You do not need to chant twelve names; you need to know **which signal word demands which form**.

### Signal words: the fastest marks
| Signal | Tense it demands | Example |
|---|---|---|
| yesterday, ago, last year, in 2010 | simple past | She **moved** last year. |
| since + point of time | perfect (continuous) | I **have known** him since 2015. |
| for + period | perfect (continuous) | We **have lived** here for ten years. |
| just, already, yet, so far, recently | present perfect | He has **just left**. |
| now, look!, listen! | present continuous | Look! It **is raining**. |
| every day, usually, often | simple present | He **walks** to school every day. |
| tomorrow, next week | future | The results **will come** tomorrow. |

*Since* points at the **start** (since Monday, since 2019); *for* measures the **length** (for three days). Mixing them is a planted error.

### Two hard rules the exam loves
**1. No future inside a time or condition clause.** After *when, as soon as, before, after, until, if, unless*, use the **present** tense even when the meaning is future:
- *I will call you when I **reach** home* (not *will reach*).
- *If it **rains**, the match will be cancelled* (not *will rain*).
The future appears only in the **main** clause: will + V1.

**2. The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.**
- *The patient **had died** before the doctor **arrived**.*
- *The players **had left** the field before the rain **started**.*
Simple past for the later action; had + V3 for the earlier one.

### Perfect continuous: the 'duration up to now' tense
When an action began in the past and **is still running**, use has/have been + V-ing:
- *It **has been raining** since morning.*
- *The workers **have been working** on this bridge for two years.*
If the running action ended **before another past moment**, shift one step back: had been + V-ing — *He was exhausted because he **had been walking** for six hours.*

### How to attack an item
1. Underline the signal word (ago, since, tomorrow, as soon as, before).
2. Ask: is the action finished, running, or earlier than another action?
3. Match the form, then check the other clause of the sentence for agreement with the timeline.

### Quick revision
- ago/last/yesterday → simple past; since/for/just/already → perfect family.
- since + point, for + period.
- when/if/as soon as + present (never will) in the time clause.
- Earlier past action → had + V3.
- Still running → has/have been + V-ing; finished before a past point → had been + V-ing.

patterns.name: Signal word fixes the tense
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence carries a time signal: yesterday, ago, last year, since, for, just, already, now, every day.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the signal word.
2. Read its demanded tense off the signal table.
3. Choose the option with that form and reject look-alike forms of neighbouring tenses.

*Why it works:* each signal belongs to exactly one tense family.

example.q: *She ___ to Chennai last year.* (moved/has moved/had moved/moves)
example.solution: last year → simple past → **moved**. 'Has moved' would need a since/for signal.

patterns.name: No future in the time or if clause
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence pairs a future main clause (will ...) with a clause beginning when/if/as soon as/until/unless/before.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the time/condition word.
2. Inside that clause use the present tense even for future meaning.
3. Keep will only in the main clause.

*Why it works:* English treats the time clause as a timetable entry — present form, future sense.

example.q: *I will call you when I ___ home.* (reach/will reach/reached/am reaching)
example.solution: Time clause → present → **reach**.

patterns.name: Past perfect for the earlier past action
patterns.howToSpot: Two past actions with before/after/when joining them; the options mix had + V3 and V2.
patterns.logic:
1. Put the two actions on a timeline.
2. The earlier one gets had + V3; the later one gets simple past.
3. Check the before/after direction before choosing.

*Why it works:* the past perfect exists precisely to mark 'earlier past'.

example.q: *The patient had died before the doctor ___.* (arrived/had arrived/arrives)
example.solution: Death happened first (already in past perfect) → doctor later → **arrived**.

patterns.name: Perfect continuous with since/for
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence measures an action's duration (since morning, for two years) and the action is still going on.
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm duration + still running → has/have been + V-ing.
2. If the frame is past (was exhausted yesterday), step back to had been + V-ing.
3. Reject plain continuous and simple forms.

*Why it works:* only the perfect continuous family can carry 'from then until now'.

example.q: *He was exhausted because he ___ for six hours.*
example.solution: Running before a past point → **had been walking**.

subtopics.title: Subject-verb agreement (all rules and exceptions)
subtopics.concept:
Subject-verb agreement (SVA) is the single most tested grammar point in SSC error spotting. The rule is simple (singular subject → singular verb), but the traps are in **finding the real subject**.

| # | Rule | Correct example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Find the head noun; ignore phrases after *of, in, with* etc. | The **quality** of the apples **is** poor. |
| 2 | A and B → plural | Ravi and his sister **are** here. |
| 3 | A and B = one person/idea (one article) → singular | The secretary and treasurer **has** resigned. / Bread and butter **is** my breakfast. |
| 4 | *each / every* before A and B → singular | Every boy and every girl **was** given a prize. |
| 5 | A **as well as / along with / together with / with / besides / in addition to / rather than / accompanied by / including / like / no less than** B → verb agrees with **A** | The minister, along with his aides, **was** present. |
| 6 | **either...or / neither...nor / not only...but also / or / nor** → verb agrees with the **nearer** subject | Neither the teacher nor the students **were** late. |
| 7 | *each, every, either, neither, everyone, someone, anyone, no one, nobody, everything* → singular | Each of the players **has** a kit. |
| 8 | *one of + plural noun* → singular verb | One of my friends **is** a pilot. |
| 9 | *one of those + plural noun + who/that* → plural verb (the relative clause describes the group) | He is one of those people who **never give** up. |
| 10 | *the only one of ... who* → singular | She is the only one of the girls who **has** passed. |
| 11 | **A number of** → plural; **the number of** → singular | A number of cars **were** towed. The number of cars **is** rising. |
| 12 | *many a* + singular noun → singular | Many a man **has** tried. |
| 13 | *more than one* + singular noun → singular | More than one student **was** absent. |
| 14 | Amount of money/time/distance/weight as one unit → singular | Fifty rupees **is** too much for this. Ten km **is** a long way. |
| 15 | *half / part / some / all / most / plenty / a lot / rest / % / fractions* **of** X → verb agrees with X | Half of the cake **is** eaten. Half of the guests **are** here. |
| 16 | Titles, names of countries/organisations, even if plural in form → singular | The United Nations **is** based in New York. |
| 17 | *the + adjective* (class of people) → plural | The rich **are** not always happy. |
| 18 | *There / Here* + verb: verb agrees with the noun that follows | There **are** many reasons. Here **comes** the bus. |
| 19 | Gerund, infinitive or noun clause as subject → singular | Walking **is** good exercise. What he said **was** false. |
| 20 | Relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent | I, who **am** your friend, will help. |
| 21 | *a pair of / a series of / a set of* + plural noun → singular (head is pair/series/set) | A pair of shoes **was** stolen. |
| 22 | Uncountable nouns → singular; always-plural nouns → plural | The furniture **is** new. My trousers **are** torn. |

### Collective nouns
*team, committee, jury, family, staff, audience, crowd, board, government* take a **singular** verb when acting as one body and a **plural** verb when the members act separately: *The team **is** strong* / *The team **are** arguing among themselves*. A matching pronoun follows the same choice (*its* vs *their*).

### Tricky subjects summary
- **Singular**: news, mathematics, economics (subject), measles, furniture, information, luggage, scenery, *each, every, either, neither*, amounts as a unit, titles.
- **Plural**: cattle, police, people, poultry, clergy, scissors, trousers, spectacles, *the rich / the poor*, *a number of*, *both, few, many, several*.
- **Depends on the noun after *of***: *all, some, most, half, none (with uncountable → singular), a lot, plenty, the rest, 40 per cent, two-thirds*.

tricks.title: Strike-through method
tricks.body: Draw a line through every **prepositional phrase** (*of the boys, in the box, with his friends*) and every **add-on phrase** (*as well as..., along with..., together with...*). What remains before the verb is the true subject.

example.q: The captain, together with his players, ___ (was/were) felicitated.
example.solution: Strike *together with his players* → *The captain ___ felicitated* → **was**.

tricks.title: Nearest-noun rule for or/nor pairs
tricks.body: For *either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, or, nor*: look **only** at the subject closest to the verb. Tip: put the plural subject second so the plural verb sounds natural.

example.q: Either the players or the coach ___ (is/are) responsible.
example.solution: Nearest subject *the coach* (singular) → **is**.

tricks.title: Number vs A number
tricks.body: ***The** number* = one figure (singular). ***A** number* = many (plural). Memory hook: *A = Abundant*.

mistakes: Matching the verb with the noun just before it (*The list of items are...*) instead of the head noun.
Treating *as well as / along with* like *and* and using a plural verb.
Using a plural verb after *each / every / either / neither*.
Using a singular verb after *one of those who*; the relative clause refers to the plural group.
Treating *people / police / cattle* as singular.
Using a plural verb for a sum of money or distance treated as one amount.
subtopics.notes:
### The one rule behind every item
A verb agrees with its **real subject** in number: singular subject → singular verb (has, is, was, does), plural subject → plural verb (have, are, were, do). The whole subtopic is about finding the real subject when something stands between it and the verb.

### Rule 1: ignore the phrase before the verb
Words glued to the subject with *of, with, along with, as well as, together with, besides, in addition to, accompanied by* do **not** change its number:
- *The quality **of the mangoes** **was** good.* (subject = quality)
- *The principal, **as well as** the teachers, **was** present.* (subject = principal)
- *The list **of candidates** **has** been published.*
Cover the prepositional phrase with your finger and match the verb to what remains.

### Rule 2: each, every, everyone, either — always singular
- *Each **of the girls** **was** given a certificate.*
- *Every one **of the players** **was** praised.*
- *Neither answer **is** correct.*
Even when a plural noun follows *of*, the words each, every, everyone, everybody, anyone, either, neither keep the verb singular.

### Rule 3: neither...nor / either...or — the verb follows the NEARER subject
- *Neither the manager **nor the workers** **were** present.* (workers = plural, nearer)
- *Either Ram **or his brothers** **are** to blame.*
Think of it as proximity: the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

### Rule 4: collective nouns and special singulars
- Collective nouns (committee, team, jury, family, audience) take a **singular** verb when the group acts as one: *The committee **announced** its decision.*
- Subjects ending in -ics (mathematics, physics, economics, politics as a field) are singular: *Mathematics **is** my favourite subject.*
- **More than one** + singular noun → singular verb: *More than one student **was** selected.*
- Amounts of money, distance, time as one unit → singular: *Ten kilometres **is** a long walk.*

### Finding the error fast
In divided-part items, the error is nearly always in the verb part. Read the first part, strike the *of/as well as* phrase, ask singular or plural, and test the verb. In fill-blank items, the options are usually has/have, is/are or was/were — the same test decides.

### Quick revision
- Cover of/with/as well as phrases; the head noun rules.
- each/every/everyone/either/neither (alone) → singular.
- neither...nor, either...or → verb follows the nearer subject.
- Committee, mathematics, more than one, ten kilometres → singular.
- The error part usually carries the verb.

patterns.name: Head noun before an 'of' phrase
patterns.howToSpot: A phrase like *the quality of, the list of, the bouquet of, one of the* sits before the verb.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the true head noun (quality, list, bouquet, one).
2. Ignore the of-phrase entirely.
3. Match the verb to the head noun's number.

*Why it works:* of introduces a description, not a second subject.

example.q: *The bouquet of roses ___ on the table.* (is/are/were/have)
example.solution: Head noun = bouquet (singular) → **is**.

patterns.name: Each, every and one of: fixed singular
patterns.howToSpot: The subject begins with each, every, everyone, everybody, either, neither, or 'one of the ...'.
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm the subject word is on the singular list.
2. Choose the singular verb even if a plural noun follows of.
3. Reject the plural option that 'sounds' natural.

*Why it works:* these words point to members one at a time, so English keeps the verb singular.

example.q: *Each of the girls ___ given a certificate.* (was/were/are/have)
example.solution: Each → singular → **was**.

patterns.name: Proximity rule for neither...nor / either...or
patterns.howToSpot: Two subjects are joined by neither...nor, either...or, or not only...but also, and they differ in number.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the subject NEARER the verb.
2. Match the verb to that subject alone.
3. Ignore the farther subject completely.

*Why it works:* the proximity rule overrides both subjects' individual numbers.

example.q: *Neither the manager nor the workers ___ present.* (were/was/is/has)
example.solution: Nearer subject = workers (plural) → **were**.

patterns.name: Collective nouns and special singular subjects
patterns.howToSpot: The subject is a collective noun (committee, team), an -ics subject, 'more than one ...', or an amount (ten kilometres).
patterns.logic:
1. Check the special-singular list.
2. Group acting as one unit → singular verb.
3. Choose the singular form and ignore the plural look of the nearest noun.

*Why it works:* these subjects name one unit or one idea, whatever their shape.

example.q: *More than one student ___ selected.* (was/were/have/are)
example.solution: More than one → singular → **was** — a planted surprise.

subtopics.title: Articles (a, an, the, zero article) and determiners
subtopics.concept:
### A or An: go by the first SOUND, not the letter
| Use **an** (vowel sound) | Use **a** (consonant sound) |
|---|---|
| an hour, an honest man, an heir, an honour | a university, a unit, a European, a useful tip |
| an MLA, an MBA, an SP, an X-ray, an LLB | a one-day match, a one-way street, a ewe, a union |
| an FIR, an NGO, an 8-year-old | a U-turn, a uniform, a hotel (h is sounded) |

Letters whose names begin with a vowel sound: **A, E, F, H, I, L, M, N, O, R, S, X** → *an F-grade, an M.Sc., an S-bend*.

### Uses of A / An
- First mention of a countable singular: *I saw **a** cat.*
- Profession or class: *She is **a** doctor.*
- Rate: *60 km **an** hour, twice **a** week, ₹50 **a** kilo*.
- Exclamations and fixed phrases: *What **a** sight! such **a** fool, quite **a** crowd, half **an** hour, **a** few, **a** little, **a** lot of, **a** great deal of, in **a** hurry, as **a** rule, at **a** loss*.

### Uses of The
| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| Something already mentioned or specific | *I bought a pen. **The** pen leaks.* |
| Unique objects | *the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth, the world* |
| Superlatives and ordinals | *the best, the first, the last, the only, the same* |
| Rivers, seas, oceans, canals, gulfs | *the Ganga, the Arabian Sea, the Pacific, the Suez Canal* |
| Mountain ranges, island groups, deserts | *the Himalayas, the Andamans, the Thar* |
| Holy books, epics, newspapers, famous buildings | *the Gita, the Ramayana, the Hindu, the Taj Mahal* |
| Countries with Republic/Union/States/plural names | *the USA, the UK, the Netherlands, the Maldives* |
| Musical instruments | *She plays **the** sitar.* |
| Adjective used as a class of people | *the rich, the poor, the blind* |
| Whole species (singular noun) | ***The** tiger is a national animal.* |
| Double comparative | ***The** more you read, **the** better you write.* |
| Proper noun used as common noun | *Kalidas is **the** Shakespeare of India.* |
| Directions | *in **the** north* (but *go north*) |

### No article (zero article)
- Proper nouns of people, cities, most countries, single mountains, single lakes: *Mount Everest, Lake Chilika, India*.
- Languages and school subjects: *He speaks **Hindi**; **physics** is hard.*
- Meals, games, most diseases: *have **lunch**, play **cricket**, suffer from **malaria*** (but *a heavy lunch, the flu, a cold, a headache*).
- Abstract and material nouns in a general sense: ***Honesty** is the best policy; **Gold** is costly* (but ***The** gold of Kolar*).
- *man* meaning mankind: ***Man** is mortal.*
- Institutions used for their main purpose: *go to **school / church / hospital / prison / bed / college*** (but *went to **the** school to meet the principal*).
- Transport with *by*: *by bus, by train, by air*; time phrases: *at night, next week, last year, by chance, in time*.

### Determiners quick table
| Word | With | Note |
|---|---|---|
| each | singular, from a known group (2+) | *each side of the road* |
| every | singular, 3+ as a whole | *every student* |
| some / any | *some* in positive, *any* in negative/questions | *Some* in offers: *Would you like some tea?* |
| much / little / less | uncountable | *much time, less water* |
| many / few / fewer | countable plural | *many books, fewer errors* |

tricks.title: Say it aloud
tricks.body: For a/an, whisper the next word. If your mouth starts with a vowel **sound** (*on-est, em-el-ay, ex-ray*), use **an**; if it starts with *y* or *w* sound (*you-niversity, won-day*), use **a**.

example.q: He is ___ one-eyed man and ___ honest worker.
example.solution: *one* sounds *won* → **a** one-eyed man; *honest* sounds *on-est* → **an** honest worker.

tricks.title: The geography rule of thumb
tricks.body: **Plural or water or chain → THE** (the Alps, the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Andamans). **Single peak, single lake, city, most countries → no article** (Mount Abu, Lake Dal, Delhi, Nepal).

mistakes: Choosing a/an by spelling: *an university, a hour, an European* ✗.
Using *the* with meals, games and languages: *play the cricket, the English is easy* ✗.
Dropping *the* before superlatives or *same/only*.
Using *the* with single mountains or lakes: *the Mount Everest* ✗.
Omitting *a* in rate expressions and fixed phrases: *twice week, in hurry* ✗.
subtopics.notes:
### A or An: trust the first SOUND
Choose a or an by the **sound** the next word begins with, never by its spelling:
- **an** before vowel sounds: an hour, an honest man, an heir, an M.A., an MLA, an X-ray.
- **a** before consonant sounds: a university, a European, a one-rupee coin, a unique idea.
*University* begins with the sound 'yu' (a consonant sound); *hour* begins with a silent h. That is the whole game, and the exam plants these exact words.

### Where THE is compulsory
1. **Second mention**: *A king came. **The** king was just.*
2. **Unique things**: the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth, the equator.
3. **Superlatives and ordinals**: the best novel, the first attempt, the only chance.
4. **Rivers, seas, mountain ranges, island groups, deserts**: the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Sahara.
5. **Directions**: the east, the north.
6. **The + adjective = the whole class**: *The rich are not always happy.*

### Where NO article goes (zero article)
- **Languages and subjects**: English, French, mathematics, history.
- **Meals**: have breakfast, at lunch, after dinner.
- **School, college, church, prison, hospital, bed** when used **for their purpose**: *He goes to school every day* (as a student) vs *He went to the school to meet the headmaster* (the building).
- **Man and mankind** in the sense of the human race: *Man is mortal.*
- **General plurals**: *Books are our best friends.*
Planted error: *The man is mortal* → drop *The*.

### Few, a few, little, a little
| Word | Sense | Used with |
|---|---|---|
| few / a few | hardly any / some | countable plurals (friends, days) |
| little / a little | hardly any / some | uncountables (time, hope, money) |
*A few friends* = some friends (positive); *few friends* = almost none (negative). The sentence's sense decides: *He is new in the city and has **few** friends here.*

### Attacking an item
1. Hear the first sound of the next word → a/an settles.
2. Look for the the-triggers: second mention, unique, superlative, rivers, the + adjective.
3. If a language, meal or purpose-building has an article, that part is the error.

One more exam habit: when the options are a/an/the/no-article, say the whole noun phrase aloud before marking. *an university* and *a hour* stumble on the tongue, and the ear catches what the eye forgives.

### Quick revision
- an hour, an MLA, an honest man; a university, a European, a one-rupee coin.
- the: second mention, unique things, superlatives, rivers, directions, the + adjective.
- no article: languages, meals, school-for-study, man (human race), general plurals.
- few/little = hardly any; a few/a little = some.

patterns.name: A vs An by first sound
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits before a word whose spelling and sound disagree: hour, honest, heir, university, European, one-..., M.L.A., X-ray.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the next word aloud and catch its first sound.
2. Vowel sound → an; consonant sound → a.
3. Reject the option chosen by spelling.

*Why it works:* the rule is about sound flow, and the exam words are a fixed set.

example.q: *She is ___ MLA from Bihar.* (an/a/the/one)
example.solution: MLA begins with the sound 'em' → **an**.

patterns.name: Compulsory THE
patterns.howToSpot: The blank precedes a unique thing, a superlative, a river or range, a direction, or a second mention.
patterns.logic:
1. Check the the-triggers: unique, superlative, second mention, geographical name, direction, adjective as class.
2. If one fires, choose the.
3. Otherwise consider a/an or zero.

*Why it works:* the marks a specific, identified thing; each trigger identifies it.

example.q: *___ Ganga is a holy river.* (The/A/An/No article)
example.solution: River names take the → **The Ganga**.

patterns.name: Zero article traps
patterns.howToSpot: An article sits before a language, a meal, a purpose-building, or 'man/mankind'; or the sentence compares school and the school.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask if the noun is used for its purpose (go to school = study).
2. Languages, meals and mankind take no article.
3. In divided parts, the article-bearing part is the error.

*Why it works:* purpose-use nouns behave like abstract ideas, not concrete places.

example.q: *The man is mortal.* — improve the sentence.
example.solution: Man = the human race → **Man is mortal**; drop The.

patterns.name: Few / a few, little / a little
patterns.howToSpot: The blank precedes a countable plural (friends, days) or an uncountable (time, hope), and the options are few/a few/little/a little.
patterns.logic:
1. Countable plural → few family; uncountable → little family.
2. Read the sentence's sense: positive (some) → a few / a little; negative (almost none) → few / little.
3. Match the option.

*Why it works:* a makes the difference between 'some' and 'hardly any'.

example.q: *Give me ___ time to think; I'm almost done.* (a little/little/the little/a few)
example.solution: Almost done → needs a short positive amount → **a little**.

subtopics.title: Prepositions and conjunctions
subtopics.concept:
### Prepositions of time and place
| Preposition | Time | Place |
|---|---|---|
| **at** | exact point: *at 6 pm, at noon, at night, at dawn* | point/address: *at the gate, at 12 MG Road* |
| **on** | days and dates: *on Monday, on 15 August* | surface/street: *on the table, on MG Road* |
| **in** | months, years, seasons, parts of day: *in May, in 2025, in the evening* | enclosed area/city/country: *in the room, in Delhi* |
| **by** | not later than: *by 5 pm* | beside/means: *by the window, by train* |
| **till / until** | up to (continuity): *wait till 5* | - |
| **since / for** | point / period with perfect tenses | - |
| **between / among** | two / more than two | *between the two banks, among the villagers* |
| **beside / besides** | *beside* = next to; *besides* = in addition to | *sat beside me; besides English, he knows Tamil* |
| **into / in** | *into* = movement inside; *in* = position | *jumped into the pool; swimming in the pool* |

### Fixed prepositions (collocations SSC repeats)
| Fixed combination | Sense |
|---|---|
| abide by | follow a rule |
| absorbed in | fully busy |
| accede to | agree to a request |
| accompanied by (person) / with (thing) | went along with |
| accuse of / charge with | blame for a crime |
| acquainted with | knows |
| addicted to | habit |
| afraid of | fear |
| agree with (person) / to (proposal) / on (point) | agreement |
| angry with (person) / at (thing) | anger |
| apologise to (person) for (act) | say sorry |
| aware of / conscious of | knowing |
| beware of | be careful |
| boast of | brag |
| capable of | able |
| comply with | obey |
| confident of | sure |
| congratulate on | praise for success |
| consist of | made up of |
| cope with | manage |
| deal in (goods) / deal with (handle) | trade / handle |
| depend on / rely on | trust |
| deprive of | take away |
| die of (disease) / from (cause) | death |
| differ from (thing) / with (person's view) | disagree |
| divide into (parts) / among (people) | share |
| eligible for | qualified |
| envious / jealous of | envy |
| famous for | known for |
| fond of | likes |
| good at / weak in | skill |
| guilty of | blame |
| indifferent to | not caring |
| insist on | demand firmly |
| interested in | keen |
| married to | wedded |
| object to (+ V-ing) | oppose |
| part with (thing) / from (person) | give up / leave |
| prefer X to Y | choose |
| prevent / refrain / abstain from | stop |
| proud of | pride |
| senior / junior / superior / inferior / prior to | comparison |
| similar to / identical with | likeness |
| succeed in | achieve |
| sure of | certain |
| tired of (bored) / from (exhausted) | fatigue |
| wait for (someone) / wait on (serve) | waiting |

**Verbs that take NO preposition before the object**: *discuss* (the plan), *describe*, *reach* (the station), *enter* (the room), *marry* (someone), *attack*, *resemble*, *request*, *order*, *answer* (a question), *comprise*, *emphasise*, *investigate*. *discuss about* ✗, *reach at* ✗, *comprises of* ✗ (but *consists of* ✓, *is composed of* ✓), *request for* (as verb) ✗ (but *a request for* as noun ✓).

### Conjunctions
**Correlative pairs (must be used as fixed pairs):**
| Pair | Example |
|---|---|
| either ... or / neither ... nor | *Neither he nor I knew.* |
| both ... and | *both Ravi **and** Sita* (not *both...as well as*) |
| not only ... but also | *She **not only** sings **but also** dances.* |
| whether ... or | *whether you like it **or** not* |
| no sooner ... than | *No sooner had he left **than** it rained.* |
| hardly / scarcely / barely ... when / before | *Hardly had I sat **when** the phone rang.* |
| though / although ... yet (or nothing) | *Though he is poor, (yet) he is honest.* (**never** *though...but*) |
| so ... that / such ... that (result) | *so tired **that** he slept* |
| such ... as / the same ... as (relative) | *such books **as** these* |
| lest ... should | *Walk carefully **lest** you **should** fall.* (never *lest...not*) |
| rather / other ... than | *I would rather walk **than** wait.* |
| as ... as / so ... as (negative) | *not so tall **as** his brother* |

**Conjunction errors SSC tests**
- Double conjunctions: *Although ... but*, *Because ... so*, *Since ... therefore* ✗ (use only one).
- **unless / until / lest / till** already carry a negative sense: *Unless you do **not** work hard* ✗.
- *The reason ... is **that*** (not *because*): *The reason he failed is **that** he did not study.*
- *Scarcely ... than* ✗ and *No sooner ... when* ✗: pairs cannot be mixed.
- **Parallelism**: correlatives must join the same kind of words: *He **not only** plays cricket **but also** football* ✗ → *He plays **not only** cricket **but also** football*.

tricks.title: Partner check for correlatives
tricks.body: The moment you see *hardly, scarcely, no sooner, not only, neither, either, both, whether, lest, though*, scan ahead for its fixed partner. A wrong or missing partner is the error ~80% of the time.

example.q: Spot the error: Scarcely had the match started / than it began / to rain heavily.
example.solution: *Scarcely* pairs with **when/before**, not *than* → *Scarcely had the match started **when** it began to rain.*

tricks.title: Verb-preposition memory by meaning
tricks.body: Group collocations by the idea: **stopping** (prevent/refrain/abstain/desist **from**), **dependence** (depend/rely/count **on**), **skill** (good/expert/adept **at**; proficient **in**), **Latin comparatives** (senior/junior/superior/inferior/prior/prefer **to**). One group, one preposition.

mistakes: Adding a preposition after *discuss, reach, enter, resemble, request, comprise*.
Using *between* for more than two people/things.
Writing *prefer X than Y* instead of *prefer X to Y*.
Using *though...but*, *because...so*, *both...as well as*.
Adding *not* after *unless / lest / until*.
Using *since* with a period (*since three days*) instead of *for*.
subtopics.notes:
### Prepositions: time and place
| Preposition | Time | Place |
|---|---|---|
| **at** | exact time: at 6 o'clock, at noon | exact point: at the bus stop, at the door |
| **on** | days and dates: on Monday, on 15 August | surface: on the table, on the wall |
| **in** | months, years, seasons, parts of day: in May, in 1998, in the morning | enclosed or large areas: in the room, in Bengaluru, in India |

Since vs for: *since* + starting point (since 2019, since Monday); *for* + length (for five years, for a week).

### Fixed prepositions: learn as pairs
The exam tests which preposition a particular adjective, noun or verb **demands**. Memorise the pair, not the logic:
| Word | Pair |
|---|---|
| afraid, capable, fond, accused, proud, ashamed | **of** |
| good, bad, skilled, brilliant | **at** |
| angry **at** a thing; angry **with** a person | at / with |
| married, engaged, similar, senior, junior, preferable | **to** |
| abide, comply | **by** |
| listen | **to** |
| wait, prepare, apologise | **for** |
| insist, depend, congratulate ... on | **on** |
Note *senior to* (not senior than) and *prefer tea to coffee* (not than).

### Between and among
- **between** for two (or clearly separate items): *divided between the two winners*.
- **among** for more than two treated as a mass: *distributed among the villagers*.

### Correlative conjunctions: fixed partners
Each of these works only with its partner; mixing the partners is the classic planted error:
- **No sooner ... than**: *No sooner had the bell rung **than** the students rushed out.*
- **Hardly / Scarcely ... when**: *Hardly had the match started **when** it began to rain.*
- **Not only ... but also** (both parts join parallel words): *She is not only intelligent **but also** hardworking.*
- **Neither ... nor; either ... or; both ... and** (both...and never takes a negative).
Remember: *no sooner* and *hardly* open with an inversion (had + subject) in written exam English.

### Attack method
1. Find the word the preposition hangs on (adjective, noun, verb) and recall its fixed pair.
2. For time/place, locate the exactness: point → at, day → on, month/enclosure → in.
3. For conjunctions, complete the pair mentally first, then choose the option that supplies it.

### Quick revision
- at 6 / on Monday / in May; at the door / on the table / in Bengaluru.
- since + point, for + period.
- fond of, good at, angry at a thing, angry with a person, senior to, prefer to.
- between = two, among = many.
- No sooner...than; Hardly...when; Not only...but also.

patterns.name: at / on / in for time and place
patterns.howToSpot: The blank precedes or follows a clock time, a day, a month, a city or a surface.
patterns.logic:
1. Classify the expression: exact point, day/date, month/large area, surface.
2. at → point, on → day/surface, in → month/enclosure.
3. Choose the matching option.

*Why it works:* the three prepositions partition time and space by precision.

example.q: *We reached the airport ___ 6 o'clock.* (at/on/in/by)
example.solution: Exact clock time → **at**.

patterns.name: Fixed preposition after a word
patterns.howToSpot: An adjective, noun or verb (fond, good, angry, insist, married) is followed by the blank.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the governing word.
2. Recall its fixed pair from the pair list.
3. Reject the prepositions that fit general meaning but not this word.

*Why it works:* these are conventions, and the exam reuses the same pairs.

example.q: *Ravi is very good ___ mathematics.* (at/in/on/for)
example.solution: good demands **at** for a skill.

patterns.name: Between / among and since / for confusables
patterns.howToSpot: Two or more parties share something, or a time span starts or lasts.
patterns.logic:
1. Count the sharers: two → between, many → among.
2. Point of start → since; length → for.
3. Choose accordingly.

*Why it works:* each pair splits one idea by number or shape of the span.

example.q: *The prize was divided ___ the two winners.* (between/among/in/into)
example.solution: Two winners → **between**.

patterns.name: Correlative conjunction pairs
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence opens with no sooner, hardly, scarcely or not only, and the blank is the second half of the pair.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the fixed partner: no sooner...than; hardly/scarcely...when; not only...but also.
2. Eliminate mixed partners (no sooner...when is the classic trap).
3. Choose the partner word.

*Why it works:* correlatives are welded pairs; the first half dictates the second.

example.q: *No sooner did the bell ring ___ the students rushed out.* (than/when/then/that)
example.solution: No sooner demands **than**.

subtopics.title: Modals, conditionals and the subjunctive
subtopics.concept:
### Modals: always followed by the base verb (V1)
| Modal | Main uses | Example |
|---|---|---|
| can / could | ability; *could* = past ability or polite request | *She **can** swim. **Could** you help me?* |
| may / might | permission; possibility (*might* = less likely) | ***May** I come in? It **might** rain.* |
| must | strong obligation; logical certainty | *You **must** wear a helmet. He **must** be tired.* |
| should / ought to | duty, advice (*ought* always takes *to*) | *You **ought to** respect elders.* |
| will / shall | future; *shall* for offers with I/we | ***Shall** I open the window?* |
| would | past habit; polite request; conditional | *He **would** walk daily as a child.* |
| need / dare (as modals) | only in negatives/questions, **no *to***, no *-s* | *He **need not** come. **Dare** he argue?* |
| used to | past habit that no longer exists | *I **used to** play chess.* |

- Modal + V1 only: *He can **speaks*** ✗; *She must **to** go* ✗.
- *be used to / be accustomed to* + **V-ing** (= familiar with): *I am used to **working** late* ≠ *I used to work late*.
- *had better* + V1: *You **had better** leave now.* *would rather* + V1: *I **would rather** stay.*

### Perfect modals (modal + have + V3) talk about the past
| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| must have + V3 | confident deduction | *The ground is wet; it **must have rained**.* |
| can't have + V3 | confident negative deduction | *He **can't have finished** so soon.* |
| should have / ought to have + V3 | duty not done (regret/criticism) | *You **should have told** me.* |
| could have + V3 | possible but did not happen | *We **could have won**.* |
| may / might have + V3 | possibility about the past | *She **may have missed** the bus.* |
| needn't have + V3 | did it, but it was unnecessary | *You **needn't have brought** gifts.* |

### Conditionals
| Type | If-clause | Main clause | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zero | present | present | general truth | *If you heat ice, it **melts**.* |
| First | present | will + V1 | real future possibility | *If it **rains**, we **will stay** in.* |
| Second | past (*were* for all persons) | would/could/might + V1 | unreal present/future | *If I **were** rich, I **would travel**.* |
| Third | had + V3 | would/could/might + have + V3 | unreal past | *If he **had studied**, he **would have passed**.* |

- **Never** put *will* or *would* in the *if*-clause of these patterns: *If he would have come* ✗ → *If he had come*.
- **Inverted conditionals** drop *if*: ***Had** I known = If I had known; **Were** I you = If I were you; **Should** you need help = If you need help.*
- ***unless* = if not**, so it never takes another *not*: *Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.*
- Mixed conditional: *If I **had taken** the job, I **would be** in Mumbai now* (past condition, present result).

### Subjunctive (unreal or desired situations)
- ***wish*** + past (present wish) / past perfect (past regret): *I wish I **were** taller; I wish I **had listened**.*
- ***as if / as though*** + past / *were*: *He talks as if he **were** the boss.*
- ***It is (high/about) time*** + past: *It is time we **went** home.*
- ***suggest, recommend, insist, demand, propose, order, request*** + that + subject + **(should) V1**: *The doctor suggested that he **take** / **should take** rest* (not *takes*).
- ***would rather*** + subject + past: *I would rather you **stayed** here.*

tricks.title: If-clause match table
tricks.body: Read the main clause first, then fix the *if*-clause: **will** → present; **would + V1** → past/were; **would have + V3** → had + V3. The *if*-clause is always one step 'further back' in time than the main verb.

example.q: If she ___ (leave) earlier, she would have caught the flight.
example.solution: Main clause *would have caught* → third conditional → **had left**.

tricks.title: Deduction ladder
tricks.body: Certain positive → *must have*; certain negative → *can't/couldn't have*; unsure → *may/might have*; duty missed → *should have*. Evidence words (*wet road, empty plate, lights off*) point to **must have**.

mistakes: Using *to* after a modal (*must to go*) or *-s* after a modal (*can speaks*).
Writing *would* in the *if*-clause: *If I would know...*.
Using *was* instead of *were* in the formal subjunctive (*If I was you* is informal).
Confusing *used to + V1* (past habit) with *be used to + V-ing* (familiar).
Writing *suggested that he takes* instead of *(should) take*.
Using *needn't to* or *doesn't need go*.
subtopics.notes:
### Modals: the base-verb rule
After a modal — can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must — the main verb is always the **base form (V1)**: never to + V1, never -s, never -ing.
- *He can **speak** three languages* (not speaks).
- *You should **consult** a doctor* (not to consult).
- *She need not **say** anything* (need not + V1).

### What each modal means
| Modal | Main job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| can / could | ability; could = past or polite | I can swim. Could you help me? |
| may / might | permission; possibility | May I come in? It might rain. |
| should | duty, advice, criticism of the past (should have + V3) | You should apologise. |
| must | strong obligation; strong deduction (must have + V3) | You must wear a helmet. |
| used to | past habit, now stopped | I used to play cricket every evening. |

### Perfect modals: look back at the past
modal + have + V3 judges or deduces a **past** action:
- **must have** + V3 → sure deduction: *The road is wet; it **must have rained**.*
- **should have** + V3 → it was right but not done: *You **should have taken** my permission.*
- **could have** + V3 → it was possible but did not happen: *He **could have won** with more practice.*

### Conditionals: the four patterns
| Type | If-clause | Main clause | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zero | simple present | simple present | If you heat ice, it melts. |
| First (real) | simple present | will + V1 | If it rains, the match **will be** postponed. |
| Second (unreal present) | simple past | would + V1 | If I **were** you, I **would apologise**. |
| Third (unreal past) | had + V3 | would have + V3 | If he **had prepared** well, he **would have passed**. |

The planted errors: *will* in the if-clause, *was* for the second conditional (exam answer: **were**), and *would* in the third conditional's if-clause (correct: had + V3).

### Attack method
1. Spot the modal or the if-clause first.
2. Apply the base-verb rule, or read off the conditional row.
3. For perfect modals ask: is the speaker deducing the past (must have) or finding fault with it (should have)?

The two rules that settle most items in seconds: after any modal, the next verb is bare V1; and whatever the if-clause takes, the main clause never repeats it. If the if-clause has *had + V3*, the main clause must show *would have*; if the if-clause already says *would*, the sentence is wrong by default.

### Quick revision
- Modal + V1 always: can speak, should consult, need not say.
- must have = sure past deduction; should have = past fault; could have = missed possibility.
- First: if + present, will + V1. Second: if + past, would + V1 (were). Third: if + had V3, would have + V3.
- used to = past habit.

patterns.name: Modal + base verb
patterns.howToSpot: A modal is present and the options offer to + V1, V1, V-ing or V-s forms.
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm a modal (can, should, must, need not) governs the verb.
2. Strip everything but the base form V1.
3. Reject to-infinitives and -s/-ing forms.

*Why it works:* modals themselves carry the tense, so the main verb stays bare.

example.q: *You should ___ a doctor immediately.* (consult/to consult/consulting/consults)
example.solution: should + V1 → **consult**; 'to consult' is the planted error.

patterns.name: Perfect modal of judgement
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence looks back at a past action (the road is wet; you look exhausted) and the options are must/should/could + have.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask the speaker's purpose: deduce surely (must have), find fault (should have), note a missed chance (could have).
2. Match the option.
3. Keep have + V3 after the modal.

*Why it works:* the three perfect modals split the past into three speaker attitudes.

example.q: *You ___ have taken my permission before using my laptop.*
example.solution: Fault-finding about the past → **should have taken**.

patterns.name: Conditional sentence patterns
patterns.howToSpot: An if-clause is present and the options mix will, would, had + V3 and would have + V3.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide reality: true/likely (first), imaginary present (second), imaginary past (third).
2. Read off the row: present + will; past + would; had + V3 + would have + V3.
3. Use were (not was) in the second conditional.

*Why it works:* each conditional is a fixed two-part formula; one half decides the other.

example.q: *If I ___ you, I would apologise at once.* (were/was/am/had been)
example.solution: Unreal present → second conditional → **were**.

patterns.name: Modal choice: permission, habit, possibility
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence is a polite request, a past habit, or a prediction with varying certainty.
patterns.logic:
1. Request → may/can; past habit → used to; certainty ladder: must > may/might > could.
2. Match the politeness or certainty level the sentence signals.
3. Reject modals of the wrong strength.

*Why it works:* modals encode the speaker's certainty and politeness, so the sentence's tone picks one.

example.q: *When I was young, I ___ play cricket every evening.* (used to/am used to/was used to/use to)
example.solution: Stopped past habit → **used to**.

subtopics.title: Degrees of comparison and question tags
subtopics.concept:
### Degrees of comparison
| Degree | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | *as + adj + as* (positive); *not so/as + adj + as* (negative) | *Ravi is **as tall as** Amit. He is **not so tall as** his father.* |
| Comparative | *adj-er / more + adj + than* | *Delhi is **hotter than** Shimla.* |
| Superlative | *the + adj-est / the most + adj* | *the **tallest** tower* |

**Irregular forms**: good–better–best; bad–worse–worst; little–less–least; much/many–more–most; far–farther/further–farthest/furthest; old–older/elder–oldest/eldest; late–later/latter–latest/last.

### Comparison rules SSC tests
1. **No double comparatives or superlatives**: *more better, most tallest, more costlier* ✗.
2. ***than any other* + singular noun** when the thing compared belongs to the same group: *Everest is higher than **any other peak** in the world* (without *other* it would be compared with itself).
3. **Compare like with like** (use *that of / those of* or a possessive): *The population of Mumbai is larger than **that of** Pune* (not *than Pune*). *His marks are better than **mine*** (not *than me*).
4. **Latin comparatives take *to***: *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, anterior, posterior, preferable, prefer*: *She is senior **to** me* (not *than*).
5. **Of the two → the + comparative**: *She is **the taller** of the two sisters.*
6. ***one of the* + superlative + plural noun**: *one of the **best players*** (not *best player*).
7. Absolute adjectives (*unique, perfect, ideal, complete, round, supreme*) are not compared.
8. **Double comparative for gradual change**: *The more you practise, **the** better you get.*
9. Transformation triad (same meaning):
   - *No other city in India is **as** big **as** Mumbai.* (positive)
   - *Mumbai is **bigger than any other** city in India.* (comparative)
   - *Mumbai is **the biggest** city in India.* (superlative)

### Question tags
A question tag = **auxiliary + pronoun** of the main clause, with the **opposite polarity**.
| Statement type | Tag | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Positive with auxiliary | negative of that auxiliary | *She **is** busy, **isn't she**?* |
| Negative | positive | *They **won't** come, **will they**?* |
| No auxiliary (simple present/past) | do / does / did | *He **plays** well, **doesn't he**? You **met** her, **didn't you**?* |
| *I am* | **aren't I** | *I am late, **aren't I**?* |
| *Let's* (suggestion) | **shall we** | *Let's go, **shall we**?* |
| Imperative (order/request) | **will you / won't you / can you** | *Close the door, **will you**?* |
| *Let me / Let him* (asking permission) | **will you** | *Let me help, **will you**?* |
| Negative-sense words: *never, hardly, scarcely, seldom, rarely, barely, few, little, nobody, nothing, none* | **positive** tag | *He **never** lies, **does he**? **Few** people came, **did they**?* |
| *everyone / someone / nobody / everybody* | **they** | *Everyone was happy, **weren't they**?* |
| *everything / nothing / something* | **it** | *Nothing happened, **did it**?* |
| *There is / There are* | **isn't there / aren't there** | *There is a problem, **isn't there**?* |
| *used to* | **didn't** | *He used to smoke, **didn't he**?* |
| *had better* | **hadn't** | *We had better leave, **hadn't we**?* |
| Complex sentence with *I think / I believe* | tag follows the **subordinate** clause | *I think he is right, **isn't he**?* |

tricks.title: 'Other' check in comparative sentences
tricks.body: Whenever you see *than any / than all*, ask: *Is the subject part of the group after 'than'?* If yes, *other* (or *else*) is mandatory. *Kolkata is bigger than any city in Nepal* ✓ (different group); *...than any city in India* ✗ → *any other city*.

example.q: Spot the error: Sachin scored more runs / than any batsman / in the Indian team / that season.
example.solution: Sachin belongs to the Indian team → **than any other batsman**.

tricks.title: Tag in two steps
tricks.body: Step 1: find the auxiliary (or supply *do/does/did*). Step 2: flip the polarity, remembering that *never, hardly, seldom, few, little, nobody, nothing* make the statement **negative**, so the tag is **positive**.

example.q: She seldom visits us, ___?
example.solution: *seldom* is negative; auxiliary for *visits* is *does* → **does she?**

mistakes: Double comparatives: *more stronger, most cleverest*.
Comparing a thing with a person/place: *The roads of Pune are better than Nagpur* ✗ → *than those of Nagpur*.
Writing *senior than, superior than, prefer ... than*.
Dropping *other* in *than any other*.
Giving a negative tag after *hardly / never / few*.
Using *amn't I* or *am I not* informally; the standard tag for *I am* is *aren't I*.
subtopics.notes:
### Degrees of comparison: three patterns
- **Positive**: as + adjective + as — *Ram is **as tall as** Shyam.* The negative: not as/so ... as.
- **Comparative**: adjective-er / more + adjective + **than** — *taller than, more useful than*.
- **Superlative**: the + adjective-est / most + adjective + of/in — *the tallest **in** the class*.

Two planted errors cover most questions:
1. **Double comparative** — *more costlier, more better* are always wrong: one marker only (costlier OR more costly).
2. **Wrong partner** — a comparative must carry *than*; a superlative carries *the* and a group (in the class, of all).

### 'Than any other' constructions
When the subject belongs to the group it is compared with, use **any other** so the subject is not compared with itself:
- *Mount Everest is higher than **any other** peak in the world.*
- *Delhi is larger than **any other** city in Haryana* — wait, check membership: if the subject is NOT in the group, plain 'any' works: *The Yamuna is longer than any river in Haryana* only if the Yamuna is not a Haryana river. Ask: is the subject inside the group? Inside → any other; outside → any.

### Question tags: the mirror rule
A tag copies the sentence's auxiliary, flips its **polarity**, and ends with a matching pronoun:
- *She sings well, **doesn't she**?* (positive sentence → negative tag; sings needs does)
- *They haven't finished, **have they**?* (negative → positive tag)
The pronoun replaces the subject: nobody → **they**, everybody → **they**, this/that → **it**, these/those → **they**.

### Special tags to memorise
| Sentence | Tag |
|---|---|
| Let's go for a walk | shall we? |
| Open the window | will you? |
| I am late | aren't I? |
| Nobody called | did they? |
| Nothing happened | did it? |
| He has a car (possession, Indian usage) | doesn't he? |

Note *I am → aren't I* — the only place English drops 'am not I'.

### Attack method
1. For comparison items, count the markers (more + -er = error) and check than/the + group.
2. For tags, name the auxiliary, flip it, and swap the subject for its pronoun — in that order, every time.

In divided-part items the comparison error hides in the first half (*Gold is more costlier...*), while the tag error, when it appears, is always the last part. Scan the first part for double markers and the last part for the tag, and you cover both question types in one pass.

### Quick revision
- as...as / -er than / the -est in; never more + -er together.
- Subject inside the group → than any other.
- Tag = auxiliary copy + polarity flip + subject pronoun.
- Let's → shall we; imperative → will you; I am → aren't I; nobody → they.

patterns.name: One marker only (no double comparative)
patterns.howToSpot: An option or a part reads more + -er (more costlier, more better) or a superlative with more.
patterns.logic:
1. Count the markers of comparison in the phrase.
2. Two markers (more + -er) → error.
3. Keep exactly one: costlier / more costly / the costliest.

*Why it works:* English never stacks the two ways of forming a comparative.

example.q: *Parts: Gold is more costlier / than silver, / but both are / widely used.*
example.solution: **Gold is more costlier** is the error → Gold is costlier.

patterns.name: Than any other construction
patterns.howToSpot: A superlative-style comparison names the group the subject belongs to, and the options are any / any other / all other.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask: is the subject a member of the group?
2. Member → exclude itself: any other.
3. Outsider → plain any is fine.

*Why it works:* a thing cannot be taller than itself, so the exam forces 'other'.

example.q: *Mount Everest is higher than ___ peak in the world.* (any other/any/all other/others)
example.solution: Everest is a peak → **any other** peak.

patterns.name: Standard question tags
patterns.howToSpot: A complete sentence with a comma sits before the blank; the options are auxiliary + pronoun pairs.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the sentence's auxiliary (does, have, is, will).
2. Flip the polarity: positive sentence → negative tag.
3. Replace the subject with its pronoun.

*Why it works:* every regular tag is just these three operations.

example.q: *She sings well, ___?* (doesn't she/isn't she/does she/won't she)
example.solution: sings → does; positive → negative → **doesn't she**.

patterns.name: Special tags: let's, imperative, I am, nobody
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence is a let's suggestion, a command, an I am statement, or has nobody/nothing as subject.
patterns.logic:
1. Match the sentence type to the special-tag table.
2. let's → shall we; command → will you; I am → aren't I.
3. nobody/everybody → they; nothing → it.

*Why it works:* these five tags are fixed idioms; there is no rule to derive them from.

example.q: *I am late, ___?* (aren't I/amn't I/not I/don't I)
example.solution: The fixed tag for I am → **aren't I**.

subtopics.title: Non-finites (infinitive, gerund, participle), inversion and parallelism
subtopics.concept:
### Infinitive (to + V1) and bare infinitive (V1)
- **Bare infinitive (no *to*)** after: modals, *let, make, see, hear, watch, feel, bid, had better, would rather, rather than*, and after *but/except* following *do*: *She made him **apologise**; He did nothing but **laugh**.*
- In the **passive**, *make / see / hear* take *to*: *He was made **to apologise**.*
- Verbs followed by **to + V1**: *agree, decide, hope, plan, promise, refuse, want, wish, expect, afford, fail, manage, offer, pretend, threaten, deserve, learn, seem, tend*.
- **too ... to** gives a negative result: *He is too tired **to walk*** (not *too tired that*).

### Gerund (V-ing used as a noun)
- Verbs followed by **V-ing**: *avoid, admit, deny, enjoy, finish, mind, miss, postpone, practise, quit, resist, risk, suggest, consider, keep, give up, can't help, feel like, appreciate*.
- ***to* as a preposition** → V-ing: *look forward to, object to, be used to, be accustomed to, with a view to, confess to, be averse to, take to, devote oneself to*: *I look forward to **meeting** you.*
- After **every preposition** use V-ing: *He is fond **of reading**; She left **without saying** goodbye.*
- Gerund as subject takes a singular verb: ***Smoking** is injurious.*

### Verbs whose meaning changes
| Verb | + to V1 | + V-ing |
|---|---|---|
| stop | stop (one activity) in order to do another: *He stopped **to drink** water* | quit the activity: *He stopped **drinking** tea* |
| remember / forget | a duty still to do: *Remember **to lock** the door* | a past action: *I remember **locking** it* |
| regret | announce bad news: *We regret **to inform** you* | feel sorry about a past act: *I regret **shouting*** |
| try | make an effort: *Try **to lift** it* | experiment: *Try **adding** salt* |

### Participles
- **Present participle (V-ing)** = active; **past participle (V3)** = passive: *a **boring** lecture* (it bores) vs *a **bored** student* (he is bored).
- **Dangling participle**: the opening participle must describe the **subject** of the main clause. *Walking along the beach, a crab bit him* ✗ (the crab was not walking) → *Walking along the beach, **he** was bitten by a crab* ✓.
- **Absolute phrase** has its own subject: *The weather **being** pleasant, we went out.*

### Inversion (auxiliary before subject)
When these words **open** a sentence, use question word order:
| Opener | Example |
|---|---|
| Never / Seldom / Rarely / Little | *Never **have I seen** such courage. Little **did he know** the truth.* |
| Hardly / Scarcely ... when | *Hardly **had we reached** when it rained.* |
| No sooner ... than | *No sooner **did the bell ring** than the pupils ran out.* |
| Not only ... but also | *Not only **did she win**, but she also broke the record.* |
| Not until / Only then / Only after / Only when | *Only then **did I realise** my mistake.* |
| Nowhere / At no time / Under no circumstances / On no account / In no way | *Under no circumstances **will we accept** bribes.* |
| So + adjective ... that | *So loud **was the noise** that nobody slept.* |
| Conditional without *if* | ***Had I known**, I would have helped.* |
| Neither / Nor / So (agreement) | *He can't swim, and **neither can I**. She likes tea, and **so do I**.* |
| Here / There + verb (with a noun subject) | ***Here comes the bus*** (but *Here **it comes***) |

### Parallelism
Items joined by *and, or, but, not only...but also, either...or, both...and, than, as* must have the **same grammatical form**: *She likes reading, writing and **painting*** (not *to paint*). *He is honest, hardworking and **intelligent*** (not *has intelligence*).

tricks.title: Is 'to' a preposition? Test with a noun
tricks.body: Replace the verb after *to* with a noun. If a noun fits (*I look forward to **the holiday***), then *to* is a preposition and the verb must be **V-ing**. If only a verb fits (*I want to ~~the holiday~~*), use **to + V1**.

example.q: She is accustomed to ___ (work) late.
example.solution: *accustomed to the noise* works, so *to* is a preposition → **working**.

tricks.title: Negative opener = question order
tricks.body: If a sentence begins with a negative or restrictive word (*never, seldom, hardly, no sooner, not only, only then, little, nowhere*), immediately check that the auxiliary comes **before** the subject. Missing inversion is the planted error.

example.q: Spot the error: Rarely we have seen / such a spectacular / display of fireworks.
example.solution: *Rarely* opens the sentence → inversion: **Rarely have we seen**.

mistakes: Using *to + V1* after *look forward to / object to / be used to*.
Writing *made him to go* in the active voice.
Dangling participles that make the wrong noun do the action.
Forgetting inversion after *never, seldom, not only, no sooner, only then*.
Breaking parallel structure in lists and correlatives.
Using *too ... that*; the pattern is *too ... to* or *so ... that*.
subtopics.notes:
### Non-finites: the three shapes
A non-finite verb does not change with tense or subject. Three shapes exist:
1. **Infinitive**: to + V1 — *He promised **to finish** the work.*
2. **Gerund** (-ing used as a noun): *He avoided **answering** the question.*
3. **Participle** (-ing/-V3 used as an adjective): *the **broken** chair; **Seeing** the snake, she fainted.*

### Gerund after prepositions and set verbs
After any **preposition**, the verb takes -ing: *fond of **reading**; insisted on **paying**; interested in **learning**; before **leaving***.
After these verbs, the next verb is a **gerund**: enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest, keep, practise, stop, deny, admit, consider.
*Look forward to* ends in a preposition *to*, so it takes -ing too: *I look forward to **meeting** you* (not to meet).

### Infinitive after set verbs
After these verbs, use **to + V1**: promise, decide, agree, hope, plan, refuse, learn, afford, manage, want, offer.
**Remember + to** = duty ahead (*Remember to switch off the lights*); **remember + -ing** = memory of the past (*I remember switching it off yesterday*).

### Bare infinitive (no to)
